introduction_markdown:
**GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD - General Certificate of Education Examination. JUNE 2025, ADVANCED LEVEL. English Language, Paper 2 (0730).**

Answer your questions either exclusively from **PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS)** or from **PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS)**.

**PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS) - Duration: Two and a Quarter Hours.** Instructions to candidates: ANSWER ONE QUESTION FROM EACH SECTION (Section A: Composition, Section B: Prescribed Texts, Section C: Creative Writing). ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you no marks.

**PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS) - Duration: Three Hours.** Instructions to candidates: Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will earn you little or no marks. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you little or no marks.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS) - SECTION A: COMPOSITION (20 MARKS)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (10 marks); Expression (8 marks); Accuracy (2 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.enonce_markdown: **d)** Young girls face a lot of difficulties growing up in your community. Suggest measures which could be taken to address their difficulties.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Introduction: girls' obstacles in the community.
2. Difficulties: early marriage and teenage pregnancy.
3. Difficulties: unequal treatment, heavy chores, harassment.
4. Difficulties: poverty and lack of sanitary materials.
5. Measures: sensitisation, law enforcement, practical support, education and role models.
6. Conclusion.

**Model composition (538 words)**

Growing up as a girl in many communities in Cameroon is a journey full of obstacles. Although girls are as intelligent and hard-working as boys, they meet difficulties that slow their progress and sometimes destroy their dreams. As a member of this community, I have watched my sisters, cousins and classmates struggle, and I believe that these problems can be solved if we act together.

The first difficulty is early marriage. In some families, a girl of fourteen is given away to an older man because her parents want the bride price or fear that she will become pregnant out of marriage. Once married, she must leave school, bear children early and depend entirely on her husband. Closely linked to this is teenage pregnancy, which results from poverty, ignorance and the lack of guidance from parents. A pregnant schoolgirl is often expelled or ashamed to return, and her future is changed for ever.

A second problem is the unequal treatment of boys and girls. When money for school fees is scarce, many parents send the boys to school and keep the girls at home, believing that a girl's place is in the kitchen. Even those who attend school have to fetch water, cook and look after younger children before they can open their books. They arrive late and tired, and their results suffer. Moreover, girls face harassment from men who promise gifts in exchange for favours, as well as from some teachers who abuse their position.

Finally, poverty and ignorance about the body create further trouble. Some girls miss classes every month because they cannot afford sanitary pads, and others are never told how to protect their health.

Fortunately, several measures can be taken to address these difficulties. First, parents and community leaders must be sensitised. Meetings in the chief's palace, churches, mosques and village halls should explain that educating a girl benefits the whole family and the nation. Traditional rulers, who are respected by everyone, could declare that no girl in the village will be married before the age of eighteen.

Second, the government and local councils should enforce the laws that protect children. Those who force a minor into marriage or abuse a pupil should be punished, and a hotline should be created so that victims can report safely. Schools ought to appoint trained counsellors, and teachers who harass girls should be dismissed.

Third, financial and practical support is needed. Scholarships, free school supplies and cheap or free sanitary materials would allow poor girls to stay in school. Building schools near the villages and providing safe transport would reduce the risks of long and lonely journeys. Boys should also be taught to respect girls and to share domestic work, so that the burden is lighter.

Fourth, education about health and life skills must be improved. Girls' clubs, led by successful women of the area, can give advice, encourage ambition and show that a girl can become a doctor, an engineer or a minister.

In conclusion, the difficulties of young girls are real, but they are not unavoidable. If parents, teachers, leaders and the government play their roles, the girls of our community will grow up healthy, educated and confident, and the whole community will be stronger.

**Marking grid (the paper prints the split of the 20 marks)**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 10 | A relevant treatment of the topic as set, a clear introduction, paragraphs that each develop one idea, a logical order and a conclusion |
| Expression | 8 | Varied sentence structures, precise vocabulary, suitable register and tone, good use of linking words, a convincing style |
| Accuracy | 2 | Correct grammar, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Writing fewer than 500 or more than 550 words, or ignoring the topic's exact wording (for example listing points instead of telling a story, or giving only one side when asked 'Do you agree?').
2. A weak plan: a long introduction, paragraphs that repeat one idea, no conclusion; or a pre-prepared composition that does not fit the question (it earns no marks).
3. Giving only the difficulties, or only vague slogans such as 'the government must do something': the question asks for measures, so each one must say who does what.
